concepts.name: Factorial basics
concepts.description: n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 1 = n × (n − 1)!, with 0! = 1. Ratios of factorials cancel down to a short product.

concepts.name: Trailing zeros
concepts.description: Each zero at the end of n! needs a 2 and a 5. Fives are scarcer, so count them: ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + ⌊n/125⌋ + … Some zero counts never occur, because the count jumps at multiples of 25.

concepts.name: Highest power of a prime in n!
concepts.description: The power of a prime p in n! is ⌊n/p⌋ + ⌊n/p²⌋ + ⌊n/p³⌋ + … (Legendre): multiples of p each give one p, multiples of p² one more, and so on.

concepts.name: Highest power of a composite number
concepts.description: Split the divisor into prime powers, find each prime’s power in n!, divide by the exponent the divisor needs, and take the smallest result.

concepts.name: Sums of factorials
concepts.description: From 5! on every factorial ends in 0, and from 10! on in 00, so only the first few terms decide unit digits, last two digits and small remainders.

concepts.name: Size and digits of n!
concepts.description: n! grows faster than any fixed power aⁿ. Benchmarks such as 10! = 36,28,800 and adding logarithms give its number of digits.

concepts.name: Divisibility of factorials
concepts.description: m divides n! exactly when n! holds every prime power of m. The smallest such n is set by the prime power that takes longest to build up.

formulas.title: Factorial
formulas.prompt: How is n! defined, and what is 0!?
formulas.explanation: Writing n! as n × (n − 1)! is what makes ratios cancel. 0! = 1 keeps the rule n! = n × (n − 1)! true at n = 1.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing the numbers inside the factorial: 8! ÷ 6! is not (8 ÷ 6)!.

formulas.title: Ratio of factorials
formulas.prompt: What is the fast way to work out n! ÷ (n − k)!?
formulas.formula: n! ÷ (n − k)! = n × (n − 1) × … (k factors, counting down from n)
formulas.explanation: Everything from (n − k) downwards cancels, leaving exactly k factors.
formulas.commonMistake: Taking one factor too many or too few: 15! ÷ 12! has 3 factors, not 4.

formulas.title: Trailing zeros of n!
formulas.prompt: How many zeros does n! end in?
formulas.explanation: A zero needs a factor 10 = 2 × 5. There are always more 2s than 5s, so the 5s decide. Multiples of 25 carry a second 5, multiples of 125 a third.
formulas.commonMistake: Stopping at ⌊n/5⌋ and missing the extra fives in 25, 50, 75, …
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many zeros does 130! end in?

formulas.title: Divide by 5 again and again
formulas.prompt: What is the quickest way to add ⌊n/5⌋ + ⌊n/25⌋ + … in your head?
formulas.formula: Divide n by 5, drop the remainder; divide the result by 5 again; add every quotient
formulas.explanation: ⌊⌊n/5⌋/5⌋ = ⌊n/25⌋, so each quotient is the next term. No need to divide by 25 or 125 directly.
formulas.commonMistake: Keeping decimals (250 ÷ 5 ÷ 5 ÷ 5 = 2, but 99 ÷ 5 = 19.8 must become 19 before dividing again).
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many zeros does 600! end in?

formulas.title: Zero counts that never happen
formulas.prompt: Can n! end in any number of zeros you like?
formulas.formula:
The zero count jumps by 2 at each multiple of 25 (by 3 at multiples of 125)
The counts jumped over are never reached
formulas.explanation: Going from (25k − 1)! to (25k)! adds two 5s at once, so one count is skipped; at multiples of 125 two counts are skipped.
formulas.example:
24! ends in 4 zeros, 25! in 6
No factorial ends in exactly 5 zeros
formulas.commonMistake: Answering "5 values of n" for every possible zero count without checking for a jump.
formulas.applicationPrompt: For how many values of n does n! end in exactly 11 zeros?

formulas.title: Power of a prime in n!
formulas.prompt: What is the highest power of a prime p that divides n!?

variables.meaning: x rounded down to a whole number

formulas.explanation: Every multiple of p up to n gives one p; multiples of p² give a second, multiples of p³ a third. Each term counts one layer.
formulas.commonMistake: Using it for a composite such as 6 or 12 directly; it works only for primes.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What is the highest power of 2 in 40!?

formulas.title: Power of a composite in n!
formulas.prompt: How do you find the highest power of a composite number such as 12 that divides n!?
formulas.formula: m = pᵃ × qᵇ: power of m = smaller of ⌊Eₚ ÷ a⌋ and ⌊E_q ÷ b⌋
formulas.explanation: Each copy of m uses a copies of p and b copies of q. Whichever prime runs out first decides how many copies fit.
formulas.commonMistake: Assuming the largest prime always decides: for 12 in 30! it is the 2², not the 3.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What is the highest power of 18 that divides 40!?

formulas.title: Unit digit of a sum of factorials
formulas.prompt: What is the unit digit of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + n! for n ≥ 4?
formulas.formula:
1! + 2! + 3! + 4! = 33
n! ends in 0 for n ≥ 5, so the sum ends in 3
formulas.explanation: 5! = 120 and every later factorial contains 2 × 5, so they add nothing to the unit digit.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the unit digits of every term up to n instead of stopping at 4!.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What is the unit digit of 1! + 2! + … + 99!?

formulas.title: Remainder of a sum of factorials
formulas.prompt: How do you find the remainder of 1! + 2! + … + n! on division by d?
formulas.formula: Stop at the first k! that d divides; add the terms before it and reduce
formulas.explanation: If d divides k!, it divides every later factorial too, because they are all multiples of k!.
formulas.example:
÷ 6: 3! = 6, so only 1! + 2! = 3 is left → remainder 3
Last two digits: 10! onwards end in 00 → 1! + … + 9! ends in 13
formulas.commonMistake: Stopping at d! instead of at the first factorial d divides (for d = 8 that is 4!, not 8!).
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the remainder when 1! + 2! + … + 40! is divided by 12.

formulas.title: Digits of n!
formulas.prompt: How do you count the digits of n!?
formulas.formula:
Digits of N = ⌊log₁₀ N⌋ + 1
log₁₀ n! = log₁₀ 1 + log₁₀ 2 + … + log₁₀ n
formulas.explanation: A number with d digits lies between 10^(d − 1) and 10^d. For small n, multiply out from a benchmark such as 10! = 36,28,800 instead.
formulas.commonMistake: Counting the digits of n × 10 or of n² instead of n!.

formulas.title: Smallest n with m dividing n!
formulas.prompt: What is the smallest n for which a given number m divides n!?
formulas.formula:
For each prime power pᵃ of m, find the smallest n with Eₚ(n!) ≥ a
The answer is the largest of these n
formulas.explanation: n! must contain every prime power of m at once, so the slowest prime to collect sets n. Only multiples of p add to Eₚ, so the answer is always a multiple of some prime of m.
formulas.commonMistake: Answering n = 8 for 2⁸ by matching the exponent instead of counting the 2s in n!.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What is the smallest n for which 3⁵ divides n!?

levels.title: Counting What n! Contains
levels.description: Cancel factorials, then count the fives behind the zeros and the primes behind every power.

blocks.title: A factorial contains the one before it
blocks.body: n! = n × (n − 1)!, so 7! = 7 × 6! and 0! = 1. Ratios of factorials collapse: 10! ÷ 8! = 10 × 9 = 90. Never divide the numbers inside the factorial; 10! ÷ 8! is not (10 ÷ 8)!.

blocks.title: Zeros come from pairs of 2 and 5
blocks.body:
Every zero at the end of n! is a factor 10 = 2 × 5. Even numbers supply 2s far faster than multiples of 5 supply 5s, so count the 5s.

In 30!, the multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30: six of them. But 25 = 5 × 5 holds a second 5, so 30! holds seven 5s and ends in 7 zeros.

blocks.title: Layers of a prime (Legendre)
blocks.caption: Each layer adds one more p from the numbers that hold a higher power of p. For p = 5 it counts the zeros: 100! ends in 20 + 4 = 24.

blocks.body: The zero count jumps at every multiple of 25: 24! ends in 4 zeros but 25! ends in 6. So some counts, such as 5, never happen at all.

levels.title: Factorial Formulas
levels.description: Factorials, trailing zeros, Legendre’s formula, composite powers and sums of factorials.

levels.title: Direct Factorials
levels.description: Cancel factorials, count zeros and prime powers in one step.

levels.title: Zeros and Prime Powers
levels.description: Bigger factorials, products of factorials, a composite divisor and a remainder.

levels.title: Composite Divisors and Sums
levels.description: Scarce primes, skipped zero counts and the last digits of factorial sums.

levels.title: Advanced: How Big, and Divisible by What?
levels.description: Estimate the size of n!, find the first factorial a number divides, and see why factorials make runs of composite numbers.

blocks.title: Factorials outgrow powers
blocks.body: Each step multiplies n! by a bigger number, so n! overtakes any fixed power aⁿ: 2ⁿ is ahead until n = 3, but 4! = 24 > 16 = 2⁴ and the gap only widens. Keep the benchmarks 5! = 120, 7! = 5,040 and 10! = 36,28,800 (7 digits) to estimate sizes.

blocks.title: The first factorial a number divides
blocks.body: m divides n! when n! holds every prime power of m. For 2⁸, count the 2s: 9! has 4 + 2 + 1 = 7, 10! has 5 + 2 + 1 = 8. So 10 is the smallest n. With several primes, work out each one’s smallest n and take the largest.

blocks.title: Smallest n with m dividing n!
blocks.body: n = largest over pᵃ in m of (smallest n with Eₚ(n!) ≥ a)
blocks.caption: A large prime factor usually decides at once: 990 = 2 × 3² × 5 × 11 needs 11!.

blocks.body: n! + 2, n! + 3, …, n! + n are all composite, since k divides n! + k. Factorials are how you build a long run of numbers with no prime among them.

levels.title: Challenge: Inside a Factorial
levels.description: Digits, growth and divisibility questions on factorials.

questions.question: What is 9! ÷ 7!?
questions.method: Cancel the smaller factorial.

hints.text: Write 9! so that 7! appears inside it.
What is left after 7! cancels?

commonMistakes: Computing (9 − 7)! = 2! = 2.

questions.question: How many zeros are there at the end of 75!?
questions.explanation: ⌊75/5⌋ = 15 multiples of 5, and ⌊75/25⌋ = 3 of them (25, 50, 75) carry a second 5. So 75! holds 5¹⁸, and plenty of 2s, giving 18 zeros.
questions.method: Count the fives.

hints.text: Each zero needs a 5 (2s are plentiful).
Don’t forget that 25, 50 and 75 each hold two 5s.

commonMistakes: Stopping at 15.

questions.question: What is the highest power of 2 that divides 20!?
questions.method: Add the layers ⌊n/2⌋, ⌊n/4⌋, ⌊n/8⌋, …

hints.text: Counting only the even numbers gives 10; some even numbers hold more than one 2.
Add 20 ÷ 4, 20 ÷ 8 and 20 ÷ 16 (rounded down).

commonMistakes: Counting only the even numbers (2¹⁰).

questions.question: The unit digit of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 100! is 3.
questions.explanation: 1! + 2! + 3! + 4! = 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33. Every factorial from 5! = 120 onwards ends in 0, so the whole sum ends in 3.
solutionSteps: n! ends in 0 for every n ≥ 5.
So the sum ends in 3: true.
questions.method: Only the terms before 5! matter.

hints.text: From which factorial onwards does every term end in 0?

commonMistakes: Thinking 100 terms must change the unit digit.

questions.question: Which expression is equal to (n + 1)! − n! for every whole number n?
questions.method: Write the larger factorial in terms of the smaller, then take it out as a common factor.

hints.text: Write (n + 1)! using n!.
Take n! out of both terms.

commonMistakes: Subtracting inside the factorial: (n + 1 − n)! = 1! = 1.

questions.question: How many zeros are there at the end of 1000!?
questions.explanation: Divide by 5 repeatedly: 1000 → 200 → 40 → 8 → 1. Adding the quotients: 200 + 40 + 8 + 1 = 249.
questions.method: Divide by 5 again and again and add the quotients.

hints.text: Count the fives in 1000!.
Use the layers for 5, 25, 125 and 625.

commonMistakes: Answering 200 (only ⌊n/5⌋) or 248 (missing the 625 layer).

questions.question: The highest power of 7 that divides 100! is 7ᵏ. What is k?
questions.explanation: ⌊100/7⌋ = 14 multiples of 7, and ⌊100/49⌋ = 2 of them (49 and 98) hold a second 7. k = 14 + 2 = 16.
questions.method: Legendre: ⌊n/7⌋ + ⌊n/49⌋ + …

hints.text: How many multiples of 7 are there up to 100?
Which numbers up to 100 are multiples of 49?

commonMistakes: Forgetting 49 and 98 hold 7² and answering 14.

questions.question: How many zeros are there at the end of 25! × 36!?
questions.explanation: 25! has 5 + 1 = 6 fives and 36! has 7 + 1 = 8 fives, so the product has 14 fives. There are far more 2s than that, so the product ends in 14 zeros.
questions.method: Zeros of a product = fives of the product (when 2s are plentiful).

hints.text: Count the fives in each factorial separately.
Fives multiply into the product, so add the counts.

commonMistakes: Giving the zeros of just one factorial (6 or 8).
Multiplying the counts (6 × 8 = 48).

questions.question: If (n + 2)! ÷ n! = 132, what is n?
questions.explanation: (n + 2)! ÷ n! = (n + 2)(n + 1), a product of two consecutive numbers. 132 = 12 × 11, so n + 2 = 12 and n = 10.
questions.method: Cancel, then spot two consecutive numbers.

hints.text: After cancelling n!, two consecutive factors remain.
Which two consecutive numbers multiply to 132?

commonMistakes: Answering 12 or 11 (a factor) instead of n.

questions.question: What is the highest power of 15 that divides 50!?
questions.explanation: 15 = 3 × 5. 50! holds 3²² (16 + 5 + 1) and 5¹² (10 + 2). Each 15 needs one 3 and one 5, so the fives run out first: 15¹².
questions.method: Count each prime and take the scarcest.

hints.text: Write 15 as a product of primes.
Count the 3s and the 5s in 50!; which runs out first?

commonMistakes: Using the count of 3s (22).
Adding the two counts (34).

questions.question: What is the remainder when 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 50! is divided by 7?
questions.explanation: From 7! onwards every term is a multiple of 7. So only 1! + 2! + 3! + 4! + 5! + 6! = 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 + 120 + 720 = 873 matters, and 873 = 7 × 124 + 5.
questions.method: Drop every term that the divisor divides.

hints.text: From which term onwards is every factorial a multiple of 7?
Add 1! to 6! and divide by 7.

commonMistakes: Answering 0 because "factorials are divisible by 7".

questions.question: The highest power of 12 that divides 40! is 12ᵏ. What is k?
questions.explanation: 12 = 2² × 3. 40! holds 2³⁸ (20 + 10 + 5 + 2 + 1) and 3¹⁸ (13 + 4 + 1). The 2s allow ⌊38 ÷ 2⌋ = 19 copies of 12 and the 3s allow 18, so k = 18.
questions.method: Copies allowed by each prime; the smallest wins.

hints.text: 12 = 2² × 3, so each 12 uses two 2s and one 3.
Find the 2s and 3s in 40!, then halve the count of 2s.

commonMistakes: Halving the 2s (19 copies) and forgetting to check the 3s.
Comparing the raw counts 38 and 18 without dividing by the exponents 12 needs.

questions.question: For how many whole numbers n does n! end in exactly 30 zeros?
questions.explanation: 124! ends in 24 + 4 = 28 zeros. 125 = 5³ adds three 5s at once, so 125! ends in 25 + 5 + 1 = 31 zeros. The counts 29 and 30 are jumped over, so no n works.
solutionSteps: The count jumps from 28 to 31: 30 never occurs.
questions.method: Find where the zero count passes 30 and check for a jump.

hints.text: Roughly how big must n be for about 30 zeros? Try n near 120.
Compare the zeros of 124! and 125!.

commonMistakes: Answering 5, as for most zero counts (a run of five consecutive n).

questions.question: What is the largest whole number k for which 72ᵏ divides 50!?
questions.explanation: 72 = 2³ × 3². 50! holds 2⁴⁷ (25 + 12 + 6 + 3 + 1) and 3²² (16 + 5 + 1). The 2s allow ⌊47 ÷ 3⌋ = 15 copies; the 3s allow ⌊22 ÷ 2⌋ = 11. So k = 11.
questions.method: Divide each prime count by the exponent 72 needs.

hints.text: Factorise 72 into prime powers.
Each copy of 72 needs three 2s and two 3s.

commonMistakes: Dividing by the wrong exponents (47 ÷ 2 or 22 ÷ 3).

questions.question: What are the last two digits of 1! + 2! + 3! + … + 200!? Enter them as a two-digit number.
questions.explanation: From 10! onwards every factorial holds 2 × 5 twice, so it ends in 00. The sum 1! + … + 9! = 1 + 2 + 6 + 24 + 120 + 720 + 5,040 + 40,320 + 3,62,880 = 4,09,113 ends in 13.
questions.method: Keep only the terms not divisible by 100.

hints.text: From which factorial onwards does every term end in 00?
Add the last two digits of 1! to 9!: 01, 02, 06, 24, 20, 20, 40, 20, 80.

commonMistakes: Stopping at 4! (that only fixes the unit digit, 3).

questions.question: Match each factorial with the number of zeros it ends in.
questions.method: Count the fives layer by layer.

hints.text: Count multiples of 5, then of 25, then of 125.
Only 125! reaches the third layer.

commonMistakes: Giving 125! 30 zeros by missing the 125 layer.

questions.question: How many digits does 12! have?
questions.method: Build up from the 10! benchmark.

hints.text: Multiply by 11 × 12 = 132.

commonMistakes: Assuming n! has about n digits.

questions.question: What is the smallest n for which n! is divisible by 1,000?
questions.explanation: 1,000 = 2³ × 5³. The 2s come early; the 5s are the bottleneck. 5, 10 and 15 give three 5s, so 15! is the first factorial with 5³ (14! has only 5²).
questions.method: Find the slowest prime power and build it up.

hints.text: Write 1,000 as a product of prime powers.
Which factorial first holds three 5s?

commonMistakes: Answering 10 by counting zeros of 10 rather than the fives in n!.

questions.question: What is the smallest n for which n! is divisible by 2¹⁰?
questions.explanation: The power of 2 in n! only rises at even n. 10! has 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 twos (so does 11!), and 12! has 6 + 3 + 1 = 10. So n = 12.
questions.method: Increase n through even numbers until E₂ reaches 10.

hints.text: Use Legendre’s count of 2s in n!.
Try n = 10 and n = 12.

commonMistakes: Answering 10 by matching the exponent.

questions.question: Select ALL the statements that are true.
questions.explanation: 10! = 36,28,800 > 10,00,000. 20! is enormous next to 2²⁰ ≈ 10 lakh. 5! = 120 < 125 = 5³. 15! ≈ 1.3 × 10¹², which is less than 10¹³. 8! = 40,320 is far below 8⁸ ≈ 1.7 crore.
questions.method: Compare against benchmarks rather than computing everything.

hints.text: Use 10! = 36,28,800 and 5! = 120 as anchors.
nⁿ multiplies n by itself every time, so it beats n!.

commonMistakes: Assuming n! always beats nᵏ for a small fixed k (5! < 5³).

questions.question: For every n ≥ 2, all of the numbers n! + 2, n! + 3, …, n! + n are composite.
questions.explanation: For 2 ≤ k ≤ n, k divides n!, so k divides n! + k. And n! + k is bigger than k, so it is composite. This gives n − 1 composite numbers in a row, which is why gaps between primes can be as long as you like.
solutionSteps: k divides n! for every k from 2 to n.
n! + k > k, so it has a factor other than 1 and itself: composite.
questions.method: Find a factor of each number from the factorial.

hints.text: Does 3 divide n! + 3 when n ≥ 3?
In general, which number obviously divides n! + k?

commonMistakes: Testing one example and stopping without seeing why it always works.

questions.question: What is the smallest n for which n! is divisible by 990?
questions.explanation: 990 = 2 × 3² × 5 × 11. The prime 11 appears in no factorial below 11!, and 11! already holds 2, 3², 5 and 11. So n = 11.
questions.method: The largest prime of m often sets n.

hints.text: Factorise 990.
Which prime factor of 990 is the largest?

commonMistakes: Answering 10 because 10! is divisible by 2, 3, 5 and 9: it misses 11.
